practice.title: -10.3 Rapid-Fire
practice.afterTopic: Streaming algorithms: reservoir sampling, heavy hitters
items: Average and worst case of Array.prototype.push? O(1) amortized / O(n). A rare resize is charged against the geometric growth since the last resize.
Worst case of Array.prototype.shift? O(n) per call, O(n²) for n calls. Every element moves down one slot; arrays cannot have holes.
Map.get on a missing key returns? undefined. If undefined is a legitimate value, use map.has(key).
Hash map worst-case lookup? O(n) — all keys in one bucket. Java bounds it at O(log n) with per-bucket trees.
Why does [] truthy break code? if (arr) is true for an empty array, unlike Python. Use arr.length.
Why is "👍".length === 2? UTF-16 code units, not code points. Use [...s] or Intl.Segmenter.
Time of Array.from(s) / [...s]? O(n) — it copies.
Two Sum on sorted input — best complexity? O(n) time, O(1) space with opposed pointers.
Two Sum on unsorted input? O(n) time, O(n) space with a Map.
Longest substring without repeats — complexity? O(n) time, O(alphabet) space.
Subarray sum = k with negatives? Prefix sums + Map, O(n). Sliding window is invalid because the sum is not monotone.
Kadane on an all-negative array? Returns the largest (least negative) element, because best starts at nums[0] and cur is never clamped at 0.
Why initialize best to nums[0]? To avoid allowing an empty subarray (sum 0), which would win on all-negative input.
Max circular subarray formula? max(kadane(nums), total(nums) − kadaneMin(nums)), with an all-negative guard.
Knapsack: why backward capacity loop? So dp[c − w] still holds the previous item's state, enforcing 0/1 semantics.
Change the loop to forward and you get? Unbounded (complete) knapsack — items can be reused.
Coin change: amount-outer vs coin-outer? Amount-outer gives unbounded reuse; coin-outer counts *combinations* rather than permutations.
Longest increasing subsequence — O(n log n) trick? Keep tails[k] = smallest tail for length k+1; binary search for the replace/append index.
Is tails an actual subsequence? No. It is a set of best tails per length; reconstruction needs a prev array.
Grid unique paths recurrence? dp[r][c] = dp[r−1][c] + dp[r][c−1]; obstacles set the cell to 0.
Why roll grid DP to one row? Each cell reads only up and left, so one row plus a left variable suffices → O(C) space.
When to loop interval DP over length, not index? Always — dp[i][j] needs dp[i][k] and dp[k][j] with i < k < j, so shorter intervals must be filled first.
Edit distance transition? Match → dp[i−1][j−1]; else 1 + min(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1], dp[i−1][j−1]).
BFS shortest path on a grid — space? O(R·C) worst case for the queue, or O(k) where k is the frontier width.
DFS cycle detection on a directed graph? Three colours: WHITE/GRAY/BLACK; a GRAY neighbour means a back edge → cycle.
Undirected cycle detection? Skip the parent edge; any other visited neighbour means a cycle.
Topological sort with Kahn — how do you detect a cycle? If the output has fewer than V nodes, the graph has a cycle.
Kahn vs DFS topological sort? Kahn is iterative and detects cycles naturally; DFS uses finish times and needs colour tracking.
Dijkstra heap variant complexity? O((V+E) log V). The array variant is O(V²) and better for dense graphs.
Why "no false negatives" for Dijkstra? It needs non-negative weights so a settled distance cannot later improve.
Bellman-Ford relaxation count? V−1 passes, then one more pass to detect a negative cycle.
Union-Find find complexity? O(α(n)) amortized with both optimizations; ≤ 4 for all practical n.
Why a doubly linked list in LRU? Unlinking a node needs its predecessor; a singly linked list cannot do it in O(1).
Does Map.get refresh LRU recency? No. Only delete then set moves the key to the end.
Heap build complexity? O(n), not O(n log n), because Σ (nodes at depth d) × d = O(n).
Why is push amortized O(1) but unshift not? Geometric growth concentrates resize cost rarely; unshift shifts on every call.
Counting sort complexity and when it loses? O(n + k). Loses when k ≫ n — e.g. 1000 values in [0, 10⁹) allocates a billion-slot array.
Radix sort on 32-bit ints? Four passes of counting sort with base 256 → O(4n).
1 << 32 in JS? 1 — the shift count is taken mod 32.
-1 >>> 0? 4294967295 (unsigned reinterpretation). Use >>> for unsigned, >> for signed.

practice.title: Scenario 1 — Latency p50 fine, p99 catastrophic
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: Histogram, not average. p50=40, p95=55, p99=4000. Averages hide this.
Per-hop latency, correlated with the request id. Which hop is slow at p99?
Connection-pool wait histogram. If a large fraction of requests wait >100 ms for a connection, the pool is the queue.
Pool utilisation time series. If it plateaus at exactly max, the pool is saturated.
Slow-query log for that window. Likely: an unindexed query that the planner only picks when statistics go stale.
pg_stat_activity — connection count per state, and long-running queries.
symptoms: A Node API serving a Postgres-backed endpoint. Median 40 ms. p99 alternates between 60 ms and 4 s. Error rate near zero. CPU 45%. No deploys correlate.
rootCause: Two interacting things: pool size of 10 against a Postgres instance whose effective capacity is 8 concurrent queries, plus a query that occasionally takes 2 s (a seq scan chosen after autovacuum updated statistics). Queueing theory says a utilisation of 0.8 already produces long waits, and a 2 s service time at 0.8 utilisation produces a multi-second p99 with almost no errors.
fix: Size the pool to Postgres capacity minus headroom (typically cores * 2 + effective_spindle_count, capped well below max_connections).
SET statement_timeout per connection so a pathological query fails instead of holding a connection for 2 s.
Add the missing index; verify with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS).
Cap queueing: tryAcquire with a timeout, return 503 + Retry-After. Unbounded queueing is what turned a slow query into a latency incident.

practice.title: Scenario 2 — "It only happens in production"
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: Compare the drift rate to the number of active Worker threads: if the drift is proportional to concurrency, you have a race.
Look at the code path: is there a SharedArrayBuffer or Atomics anywhere near the counter?
Atomics.load / Atomics.store pairs instead of Atomics.add.
Cache-line sharding: is one counter hammered by all Workers?
symptoms: A counter is correct in staging and drifts in production. Rate is proportional to concurrency. Resetting the counter "fixes" it for a while.
rootCause: A read-modify-write split across Atomics.load and Atomics.store — individually atomic, jointly not. Staging has one Worker, so the window never opens.
fix: Atomics.add, or (better) per-worker shards summed at read time, which is also faster.

practice.title: Scenario 3 — The process hangs on deploy
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: lsof -p <pid> or /proc/<pid>/fd count *after* the shutdown signal: fds stay open.
ps -L -p <pid> thread count: Worker threads or libuv pool threads still alive.
AsyncResource/async_hooks dump: which async ids are still referenced?

Does the code await server.close() before or after draining the Worker pool? If it closes the pool first, in-flight requests never finish and server.close() never resolves (it waits for existing connections).
symptoms: SIGTERM sent; the process logs "shutting down" and never exits. The orchestrator waits 30 s then sends SIGKILL. In-flight requests are lost. This happens ~1 deploy in 5.
rootCause: Shutdown ordering plus unreferenced resources. Typical: (a) server.close() is called but keep-alive connections are still open, so the callback never fires; (b) a Worker pool is terminated before the HTTP server stops accepting; (c) a setInterval is never cleared; (d) a Redis/DB client is never closed and holds a socket.
practice.reference:
```
1. Mark not-ready: remove from load balancer, keep serving.
2. Stop accepting new connections (but keep existing ones alive).
3. Stop the intake to queues; drain in-flight with a deadline.
4. Close the DB/Redis clients.
5. Clear all intervals/timers.
6. Terminate Worker pools; await exit.
7. server.close() + destroy remaining sockets after the grace period.
8. process.exit(0) as the last resort, with a logged reason.
```

practice.title: Scenario 4 — CPU at 95%, throughput flat
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: pidstat -w 1: involuntary context switches are enormous; voluntary ones are small. This is the smoking gun.
pidstat -u 1: system time is a large fraction of CPU (kernel time = switching + cache-coherence overhead).
perf stat: cache misses per instruction is high.
perf c2c or a false-sharing report: multiple threads writing adjacent cache lines.
symptoms: After adding a Worker pool of 32 to an 8-core box, throughput did not improve and p99 got worse. CPU is pegged.
rootCause: Two compounding causes. (a) Oversubscription: 32 runnable CPU-bound threads on 8 cores, so most of the time is spent preempting and re-warming caches. (b) If every thread hammers one shared counter, the coherence traffic dominates everything.
fix: Set pool size to cores (or cores − 1 to leave room for the main thread). Shard any shared state per worker and aggregate at the end. If the work is fine-grained, batch it: one postMessage carrying 1000 items instead of 1000 messages.

practice.title: Scenario 5 — Deadlock in a NestJS-style service
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: Is anything *completing*? A counter of completed requests per minute going to zero while requests are accepted is a no-progress signature — deadlock or lost wakeup, not slowness.
Thread dump / async dump: are tasks parked on a lock?

Connection-pool metrics: are all connections checked out and idle-in-transaction? That is the deadlock: a request is waiting for a connection held by another request that is waiting for something else.
Search for two awaits holding two locks, or a lock held across an HTTP call.
symptoms: Intermittent total unresponsiveness: health checks pass (a trivial route responds) but every business route times out. CPU 1%. No errors logged.
rootCause: Either an async mutex cycle, or (more likely) a connection-pool deadlock: request 1 holds connection A and waits for an HTTP response from service B; service B is waiting for a connection from the pool that request 1's transaction is blocking.
fix: Never hold a lock or a DB transaction across a remote call. Restructure: fetch first, then lock. Impose a global lock order. Add tryLock with a timeout everywhere and map failure to 503. Add a no-progress alert (completed-work-per-minute = 0).

practice.title: Scenario 6 — Memory climbs for 6 hours then OOM-kills
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: dmesg | grep -i 'killed process' or cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.events → confirms it was the kernel killer, not V8.
cat /proc/<pid>/status | grep -E 'RssAnon|RssFile' → separate anonymous (heap/Buffer) from file-cache. RssFile is reclaimable; RssAnon is not.
process.memoryUsage() sampled every minute → which of rss, heapTotal, heapUsed, external, arrayBuffers is growing? external/arrayBuffers growing means Buffers/typed arrays, not objects.
--trace-gc → is GC failing to reclaim, or not being run?
Two heap snapshots an hour apart → the dominator tree diff shows the retainers.
async_hooks-based retainer check for timers/listeners: is something accumulating registrations?
symptoms: A long-lived service grows steadily. At ~6 hours the container is OOM-killed (exit 137) with heap usage "only" 40%. No JavaScript-level Error.
rootCause: (a) external growth — Buffers or ArrayBuffers held by an in-flight cache; (b) an unbounded Map used as a cache with no eviction; (c) listener accumulation (setInterval per request, EventEmitter with unbounded listeners); (d) closures retaining a large scope via a timer that is never cleared.
fix: Fix the specific retainer. Then set --max-old-space-size below the cgroup limit so V8 collects before the kernel kills; add --max-semi-space-size=16 to cut scavenge frequency; alert on the *slope* of rss and on external.

practice.title: Scenario 7 — Intermittent EMFILE after a dependency upgrade
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: /proc/<pid>/limits → soft/hard. Then compare to a Worker *child* process: does each child_process/Worker get its own fd table? (fork duplicates the table but the limit is per-process, and the number of processes may have increased.)
/proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l grouped by target: which kind dominates? socket, pipe, anon_inode (epoll/eventfd), or real files.
Did the number of sockets per request increase? e.g. the library now opens a separate socket for DNS (dns.lookup on the threadpool) or for a keep-alive agent misconfiguration.
ss -tan | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c → are there thousands in CLOSE_WAIT? CLOSE_WAIT means your side never called close — that is a leak in your code, not in the network.
symptoms: After a library upgrade, a service starts returning 500s with EMFILE: too many open files under modest load. It used to be fine.
rootCause: Either (a) the library now leaks a socket per request (a CLOSE_WAIT accumulation), or (b) the fd *limit* is being hit by a legitimate increase in concurrent sockets, or (c) child_process was added and each child inherits 3 pipe fds plus everything else.
fix: Find and fix the CLOSE_WAIT source (usually a stream whose destroy() is not called on the error path, or a response body never consumed). Then raise the limit as a mitigation: LimitNOFILE=65536 in the systemd unit. Consider dns.resolve over dns.lookup to avoid the threadpool hop. Set maxConnections and idle timeouts.

practice.title: Scenario 8 — Wrong answer under concurrency, right answer single-threaded
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: Make it deterministic: force simultaneous arrival with a Atomics.wait barrier so all Workers hit the critical section at once.
Narrow to the smallest failing input (usually 2 items).
Is the write an INSERT with no unique constraint? Then duplicates are a *database* race, not a data race.
Is the read-then-write in application code? Then it is a check-then-act race.
symptoms: A test suite passes 100% locally (single-threaded) and fails roughly (threads−1)/threads of the time in CI with 8 Workers. The failure is a duplicated or missing row.
rootCause: Either a missing unique constraint (two Workers both observe "not present" and both insert) or a read-modify-write in application code.
fix: Database: add UNIQUE and use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING/UPDATE. Never "check then insert".

Application: sharded state with a single writer per key, or a transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or an optimistic version column (UPDATE t SET v=$new, version=version+1 WHERE id=$id AND version=$old) with a retry on zero rows affected.

practice.title: Scenario 9 — "Async made it slower"
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: process.cpuUsage() vs wall time: CPU ratio ≈ 1, so the core count is not the issue; overhead is.
Count promises created: 1,000,000 promises and 1,000,000 microtask hops.
Profile: time in promise machinery / GC, not in heavySync.
symptoms: A CPU-bound batch job was refactored from a synchronous loop to Promise.all(items.map(async (x) => heavySync(x))) and now takes 3x longer, using one core.
rootCause: Every async arrow function allocates a promise and schedules a microtask. For a 2 µs unit of work, the overhead dominates. Plus GC pressure from 1M short-lived promises.
fix: (a) Move CPU work to a Worker pool sized to cores with data sharding; (b) if you must stay on one thread, cooperative chunking: batch items into chunks sized so each chunk is ~1-10 ms, run a chunk synchronously, and yield between chunks with setImmediate; (c) profile to make sure the algorithm itself is not accidentally O(n²).

practice.title: Scenario 10 — "It works, but the numbers are wrong"
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: Which stage's output count differs from its input count? (producers and consumers disagree)
Are consumers committing offsets before or after processing? (at-most-once → silent loss)
Is there any UPDATE ... SET counter = counter + 1 in the handler, applied out of order?
Version column on the aggregate row: are there updates with a *lower* version arriving after a higher one?
symptoms: An analytics pipeline computes daily aggregates. Under a 40× replay, the totals differ by ~2%. Under normal traffic they are correct. Each stage is individually "correct".
rootCause: A mix of (a) at-most-once consumption (offset committed before processing) losing messages under crash, and (b) non-commutative out-of-order updates (counter = counter + 1 applied in delivery order rather than event-version order).
fix: (a) Commit offsets after successful processing (at-least-once) and make the handler idempotent with a processed_events unique constraint; (b) carry a monotonic per-aggregate version and apply WHERE version < incoming (upsert with a version guard), making the handler order-insensitive.

Change the loop to forward and you get? Unbounded (complete) knapsack — items can be reused.
Coin change: amount-outer vs coin-outer? Amount-outer gives unbounded reuse; coin-outer counts *combinations* rather than permutations.
Longest increasing subsequence — O(n log n) trick? Keep tails[k] = smallest tail for length k+1; binary search for the replace/append index.
Is tails an actual subsequence? No. It is a set of best tails per length; reconstruction needs a prev array.
Grid unique paths recurrence? dp[r][c] = dp[r−1][c] + dp[r][c−1]; obstacles set the cell to 0.
Why roll grid DP to one row? Each cell reads only up and left, so one row plus a left variable suffices → O(C) space.
When to loop interval DP over length, not index? Always — dp[i][j] needs dp[i][k] and dp[k][j] with i < k < j, so shorter intervals must be filled first.
Edit distance transition? Match → dp[i−1][j−1]; else 1 + min(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1], dp[i−1][j−1]).
BFS shortest path on a grid — space? O(R·C) worst case for the queue, or O(k) where k is the frontier width.
DFS cycle detection on a directed graph? Three colours: WHITE/GRAY/BLACK; a GRAY neighbour means a back edge → cycle.
Undirected cycle detection? Skip the parent edge; any other visited neighbour means a cycle.
Topological sort with Kahn — how do you detect a cycle? If the output has fewer than V nodes, the graph has a cycle.
Kahn vs DFS topological sort? Kahn is iterative and detects cycles naturally; DFS uses finish times and needs colour tracking.
Dijkstra heap variant complexity? O((V+E) log V). The array variant is O(V²) and better for dense graphs.
Why "no false negatives" for Dijkstra? It needs non-negative weights so a settled distance cannot later improve.
Bellman-Ford relaxation count? V−1 passes, then one more pass to detect a negative cycle.
Union-Find find complexity? O(α(n)) amortized with both optimizations; ≤ 4 for all practical n.
Why a doubly linked list in LRU? Unlinking a node needs its predecessor; a singly linked list cannot do it in O(1).
Does Map.get refresh LRU recency? No. Only delete then set moves the key to the end.
Heap build complexity? O(n), not O(n log n), because Σ (nodes at depth d) × d = O(n).
Why is push amortized O(1) but unshift not? Geometric growth concentrates resize cost rarely; unshift shifts on every call.
Counting sort complexity and when it loses? O(n + k). Loses when k ≫ n — e.g. 1000 values in [0, 10⁹) allocates a billion-slot array.
Radix sort on 32-bit ints? Four passes of counting sort with base 256 → O(4n).
1 << 32 in JS? 1 — the shift count is taken mod 32.
-1 >>> 0? 4294967295 (unsigned reinterpretation). Use >>> for unsigned, >> for signed.

practice.title: Scenario 1 — Latency p50 fine, p99 catastrophic
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: Histogram, not average. p50=40, p95=55, p99=4000. Averages hide this.
Per-hop latency, correlated with the request id. Which hop is slow at p99?
Connection-pool wait histogram. If a large fraction of requests wait >100 ms for a connection, the pool is the queue.
Pool utilisation time series. If it plateaus at exactly max, the pool is saturated.
Slow-query log for that window. Likely: an unindexed query that the planner only picks when statistics go stale.
pg_stat_activity — connection count per state, and long-running queries.
symptoms: A Node API serving a Postgres-backed endpoint. Median 40 ms. p99 alternates between 60 ms and 4 s. Error rate near zero. CPU 45%. No deploys correlate.
rootCause: Two interacting things: pool size of 10 against a Postgres instance whose effective capacity is 8 concurrent queries, plus a query that occasionally takes 2 s (a seq scan chosen after autovacuum updated statistics). Queueing theory says a utilisation of 0.8 already produces long waits, and a 2 s service time at 0.8 utilisation produces a multi-second p99 with almost no errors.
fix: Size the pool to Postgres capacity minus headroom (typically cores * 2 + effective_spindle_count, capped well below max_connections).
SET statement_timeout per connection so a pathological query fails instead of holding a connection for 2 s.
Add the missing index; verify with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS).
Cap queueing: tryAcquire with a timeout, return 503 + Retry-After. Unbounded queueing is what turned a slow query into a latency incident.

practice.title: Scenario 2 — "It only happens in production"
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: Compare the drift rate to the number of active Worker threads: if the drift is proportional to concurrency, you have a race.
Look at the code path: is there a SharedArrayBuffer or Atomics anywhere near the counter?
Atomics.load / Atomics.store pairs instead of Atomics.add.
Cache-line sharding: is one counter hammered by all Workers?
symptoms: A counter is correct in staging and drifts in production. Rate is proportional to concurrency. Resetting the counter "fixes" it for a while.
rootCause: A read-modify-write split across Atomics.load and Atomics.store — individually atomic, jointly not. Staging has one Worker, so the window never opens.
fix: Atomics.add, or (better) per-worker shards summed at read time, which is also faster.

practice.title: Scenario 3 — The process hangs on deploy
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: lsof -p <pid> or /proc/<pid>/fd count *after* the shutdown signal: fds stay open.
ps -L -p <pid> thread count: Worker threads or libuv pool threads still alive.
AsyncResource/async_hooks dump: which async ids are still referenced?

Does the code await server.close() before or after draining the Worker pool? If it closes the pool first, in-flight requests never finish and server.close() never resolves (it waits for existing connections).
symptoms: SIGTERM sent; the process logs "shutting down" and never exits. The orchestrator waits 30 s then sends SIGKILL. In-flight requests are lost. This happens ~1 deploy in 5.
rootCause: Shutdown ordering plus unreferenced resources. Typical: (a) server.close() is called but keep-alive connections are still open, so the callback never fires; (b) a Worker pool is terminated before the HTTP server stops accepting; (c) a setInterval is never cleared; (d) a Redis/DB client is never closed and holds a socket.
practice.reference:
```
1. Mark not-ready: remove from load balancer, keep serving.
2. Stop accepting new connections (but keep existing ones alive).
3. Stop the intake to queues; drain in-flight with a deadline.
4. Close the DB/Redis clients.
5. Clear all intervals/timers.
6. Terminate Worker pools; await exit.
7. server.close() + destroy remaining sockets after the grace period.
8. process.exit(0) as the last resort, with a logged reason.
```

practice.title: Scenario 4 — CPU at 95%, throughput flat
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: pidstat -w 1: involuntary context switches are enormous; voluntary ones are small. This is the smoking gun.
pidstat -u 1: system time is a large fraction of CPU (kernel time = switching + cache-coherence overhead).
perf stat: cache misses per instruction is high.
perf c2c or a false-sharing report: multiple threads writing adjacent cache lines.
symptoms: After adding a Worker pool of 32 to an 8-core box, throughput did not improve and p99 got worse. CPU is pegged.
rootCause: Two compounding causes. (a) Oversubscription: 32 runnable CPU-bound threads on 8 cores, so most of the time is spent preempting and re-warming caches. (b) If every thread hammers one shared counter, the coherence traffic dominates everything.
fix: Set pool size to cores (or cores − 1 to leave room for the main thread). Shard any shared state per worker and aggregate at the end. If the work is fine-grained, batch it: one postMessage carrying 1000 items instead of 1000 messages.

practice.title: Scenario 5 — Deadlock in a NestJS-style service
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: Is anything *completing*? A counter of completed requests per minute going to zero while requests are accepted is a no-progress signature — deadlock or lost wakeup, not slowness.
Thread dump / async dump: are tasks parked on a lock?

Connection-pool metrics: are all connections checked out and idle-in-transaction? That is the deadlock: a request is waiting for a connection held by another request that is waiting for something else.
Search for two awaits holding two locks, or a lock held across an HTTP call.
symptoms: Intermittent total unresponsiveness: health checks pass (a trivial route responds) but every business route times out. CPU 1%. No errors logged.
rootCause: Either an async mutex cycle, or (more likely) a connection-pool deadlock: request 1 holds connection A and waits for an HTTP response from service B; service B is waiting for a connection from the pool that request 1's transaction is blocking.
fix: Never hold a lock or a DB transaction across a remote call. Restructure: fetch first, then lock. Impose a global lock order. Add tryLock with a timeout everywhere and map failure to 503. Add a no-progress alert (completed-work-per-minute = 0).

practice.title: Scenario 6 — Memory climbs for 6 hours then OOM-kills
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: dmesg | grep -i 'killed process' or cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.events → confirms it was the kernel killer, not V8.
cat /proc/<pid>/status | grep -E 'RssAnon|RssFile' → separate anonymous (heap/Buffer) from file-cache. RssFile is reclaimable; RssAnon is not.
process.memoryUsage() sampled every minute → which of rss, heapTotal, heapUsed, external, arrayBuffers is growing? external/arrayBuffers growing means Buffers/typed arrays, not objects.
--trace-gc → is GC failing to reclaim, or not being run?
Two heap snapshots an hour apart → the dominator tree diff shows the retainers.
async_hooks-based retainer check for timers/listeners: is something accumulating registrations?
symptoms: A long-lived service grows steadily. At ~6 hours the container is OOM-killed (exit 137) with heap usage "only" 40%. No JavaScript-level Error.
rootCause: (a) external growth — Buffers or ArrayBuffers held by an in-flight cache; (b) an unbounded Map used as a cache with no eviction; (c) listener accumulation (setInterval per request, EventEmitter with unbounded listeners); (d) closures retaining a large scope via a timer that is never cleared.
fix: Fix the specific retainer. Then set --max-old-space-size below the cgroup limit so V8 collects before the kernel kills; add --max-semi-space-size=16 to cut scavenge frequency; alert on the *slope* of rss and on external.

practice.title: Scenario 7 — Intermittent EMFILE after a dependency upgrade
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: /proc/<pid>/limits → soft/hard. Then compare to a Worker *child* process: does each child_process/Worker get its own fd table? (fork duplicates the table but the limit is per-process, and the number of processes may have increased.)
/proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l grouped by target: which kind dominates? socket, pipe, anon_inode (epoll/eventfd), or real files.
Did the number of sockets per request increase? e.g. the library now opens a separate socket for DNS (dns.lookup on the threadpool) or for a keep-alive agent misconfiguration.
ss -tan | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c → are there thousands in CLOSE_WAIT? CLOSE_WAIT means your side never called close — that is a leak in your code, not in the network.
symptoms: After a library upgrade, a service starts returning 500s with EMFILE: too many open files under modest load. It used to be fine.
rootCause: Either (a) the library now leaks a socket per request (a CLOSE_WAIT accumulation), or (b) the fd *limit* is being hit by a legitimate increase in concurrent sockets, or (c) child_process was added and each child inherits 3 pipe fds plus everything else.
fix: Find and fix the CLOSE_WAIT source (usually a stream whose destroy() is not called on the error path, or a response body never consumed). Then raise the limit as a mitigation: LimitNOFILE=65536 in the systemd unit. Consider dns.resolve over dns.lookup to avoid the threadpool hop. Set maxConnections and idle timeouts.

practice.title: Scenario 8 — Wrong answer under concurrency, right answer single-threaded
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: Make it deterministic: force simultaneous arrival with a Atomics.wait barrier so all Workers hit the critical section at once.
Narrow to the smallest failing input (usually 2 items).
Is the write an INSERT with no unique constraint? Then duplicates are a *database* race, not a data race.
Is the read-then-write in application code? Then it is a check-then-act race.
symptoms: A test suite passes 100% locally (single-threaded) and fails roughly (threads−1)/threads of the time in CI with 8 Workers. The failure is a duplicated or missing row.
rootCause: Either a missing unique constraint (two Workers both observe "not present" and both insert) or a read-modify-write in application code.
fix: Database: add UNIQUE and use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING/UPDATE. Never "check then insert".

Application: sharded state with a single writer per key, or a transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or an optimistic version column (UPDATE t SET v=$new, version=version+1 WHERE id=$id AND version=$old) with a retry on zero rows affected.

practice.title: Scenario 9 — "Async made it slower"
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: process.cpuUsage() vs wall time: CPU ratio ≈ 1, so the core count is not the issue; overhead is.
Count promises created: 1,000,000 promises and 1,000,000 microtask hops.
Profile: time in promise machinery / GC, not in heavySync.
symptoms: A CPU-bound batch job was refactored from a synchronous loop to Promise.all(items.map(async (x) => heavySync(x))) and now takes 3x longer, using one core.
rootCause: Every async arrow function allocates a promise and schedules a microtask. For a 2 µs unit of work, the overhead dominates. Plus GC pressure from 1M short-lived promises.
fix: (a) Move CPU work to a Worker pool sized to cores with data sharding; (b) if you must stay on one thread, cooperative chunking: batch items into chunks sized so each chunk is ~1-10 ms, run a chunk synchronously, and yield between chunks with setImmediate; (c) profile to make sure the algorithm itself is not accidentally O(n²).

practice.title: Scenario 10 — "It works, but the numbers are wrong"
practice.afterTopic: Measuring readiness: what "can I do this in 20 minutes" means
items: Which stage's output count differs from its input count? (producers and consumers disagree)
Are consumers committing offsets before or after processing? (at-most-once → silent loss)
Is there any UPDATE ... SET counter = counter + 1 in the handler, applied out of order?
Version column on the aggregate row: are there updates with a *lower* version arriving after a higher one?
symptoms: An analytics pipeline computes daily aggregates. Under a 40× replay, the totals differ by ~2%. Under normal traffic they are correct. Each stage is individually "correct".
rootCause: A mix of (a) at-most-once consumption (offset committed before processing) losing messages under crash, and (b) non-commutative out-of-order updates (counter = counter + 1 applied in delivery order rather than event-version order).
fix: (a) Commit offsets after successful processing (at-least-once) and make the handler idempotent with a processed_events unique constraint; (b) carry a monotonic per-aggregate version and apply WHERE version < incoming (upsert with a version guard), making the handler order-insensitive.

topics.title: Hash maps
topics.description: Hash maps within Data Structures.
keyConcepts: Separate chaining. Each bucket is a list (or tree). Insert is O(1) amortized; lookup is O(1 + α) where α = m/n. Simple, robust, degrades gracefully. Python's dict, Java's HashMap pre-8.

Open addressing. All elements live in one array; probe (linearly, quadratically, or by double hashing) until an empty slot is found. No per-bucket allocation; better cache behavior; deletes need tombstones. Java's HashMap post-8, HashSet, C++ unordered_map.

Bucketed with a tree per bucket: if a bucket exceeds a threshold (8 in Java), convert it to a red-black tree. Worst-case lookup becomes O(log n) instead of O(n). This is the answer that makes "hash map worst case is O(n)" nuanced and correct for Java.
Constant-time hashing is not "constant" — it is constant only in expectation over the hash distribution.
An adversary who controls the keys can force O(n²) behavior. Java added treeification to bound this at O(log n) per bucket. Python randomizes string hashing per process specifically to defeat this.
Map in JS: keys can be objects, so hashability is identity-based; two structurally equal objects are different keys.
Map preserves insertion order. Object also does for non-integer-like keys, but integer-like keys are ordered numerically first. This trips people up: {b:1, 2:2, a:3, 1:4} iterates 1, 2, b, a.

topics.title: Big-O, including amortized analysis and the space you actually use
topics.description: Big-O, including amortized analysis and the space you actually use within Data Structures.
keyConcepts: Common confusion: O(log n) vs O(n) for recursion
Auxiliary space — extra memory you allocate beyond the input and output. [...arr] is O(n) auxiliary. A hash map is O(n) auxiliary.
In-place — O(1) auxiliary. Mutating the input array is allowed unless the problem says otherwise. It is usually the "better" answer *if* you say so.
Total space — input + auxiliary + output. Building a result array of size n means O(n) total even if auxiliary is O(1).

Call stack is space. A depth-n recursion consumes O(n) stack even when its auxiliary data structures are O(1). Interviewers count this. A recursive DFS is O(V) space; an iterative DFS with an explicit stack is also O(V) space; a BFS queue is O(V) space too (in the worst case, a wide level).

Recursion limit. In Node.js, exceeding ~10,000-15,000 frames of stack throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded. Depth-first recursion over a path-shaped input of 100,000 nodes crashes. Know the iterative fallback for deep recursion — it is a real production concern, not a hypothetical.
Worst case for one push: O(n) — you might trigger a resize that copies n elements.
Worst case for n pushes: O(n) total, because between two resizes you do many constant-time pushes, and each resize's O(k) cost is charged against the Θ(k) pushes since the last resize.
Therefore amortized cost of push is O(1), and the sequence of costs is O(1), O(1), O(2), O(1), O(3), O(1), ... — occasionally large, never superlinear in aggregate.

keyConcepts: Separate chaining. Each bucket is a list (or tree). Insert is O(1) amortized; lookup is O(1 + α) where α = m/n. Simple, robust, degrades gracefully. Python's dict, Java's HashMap pre-8.

Open addressing. All elements live in one array; probe (linearly, quadratically, or by double hashing) until an empty slot is found. No per-bucket allocation; better cache behavior; deletes need tombstones. Java's HashMap post-8, HashSet, C++ unordered_map.

Bucketed with a tree per bucket: if a bucket exceeds a threshold (8 in Java), convert it to a red-black tree. Worst-case lookup becomes O(log n) instead of O(n). This is the answer that makes "hash map worst case is O(n)" nuanced and correct for Java.
Constant-time hashing is not "constant" — it is constant only in expectation over the hash distribution.
An adversary who controls the keys can force O(n²) behavior. Java added treeification to bound this at O(log n) per bucket. Python randomizes string hashing per process specifically to defeat this.
Map in JS: keys can be objects, so hashability is identity-based; two structurally equal objects are different keys.
Map preserves insertion order. Object also does for non-integer-like keys, but integer-like keys are ordered numerically first. This trips people up: {b:1, 2:2, a:3, 1:4} iterates 1, 2, b, a.

topics.title: Big-O including amortized analysis
topics.description: Big-O including amortized analysis within Problem Solving.
keyConcepts: Common confusion: O(log n) vs O(n) for recursion
Auxiliary space — extra memory you allocate beyond the input and output. [...arr] is O(n) auxiliary. A hash map is O(n) auxiliary.
In-place — O(1) auxiliary. Mutating the input array is allowed unless the problem says otherwise. It is usually the "better" answer *if* you say so.
Total space — input + auxiliary + output. Building a result array of size n means O(n) total even if auxiliary is O(1).

Call stack is space. A depth-n recursion consumes O(n) stack even when its auxiliary data structures are O(1). Interviewers count this. A recursive DFS is O(V) space; an iterative DFS with an explicit stack is also O(V) space; a BFS queue is O(V) space too (in the worst case, a wide level).

Recursion limit. In Node.js, exceeding ~10,000-15,000 frames of stack throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded. Depth-first recursion over a path-shaped input of 100,000 nodes crashes. Know the iterative fallback for deep recursion — it is a real production concern, not a hypothetical.
Worst case for one push: O(n) — you might trigger a resize that copies n elements.
Worst case for n pushes: O(n) total, because between two resizes you do many constant-time pushes, and each resize's O(k) cost is charged against the Θ(k) pushes since the last resize.
Therefore amortized cost of push is O(1), and the sequence of costs is O(1), O(1), O(2), O(1), O(3), O(1), ... — occasionally large, never superlinear in aggregate.
